Writing: Standard English Conventions: Independent clause
A group of words that can stand alone as a sentence
Dependent clause
A clause that cannot stand alone, often starting with because or although
Comma splice
Joining two independent clauses with only a comma, which is an error
Run-on sentence
Two independent clauses joined without proper punctuation
Semicolon use
Joining two closely related independent clauses
Colon use
Introducing a list, explanation, or elaboration after a complete clause
Dash use
Setting off an interruption or emphasising a sentence element
Nonessential clause
Extra information set off by commas on both sides
Essential clause
Information necessary to identify the noun, taking no commas
Subject-verb agreement
A verb matching its subject in number
Prepositional phrase interference
Words between subject and verb that disguise the true subject
Pronoun-antecedent agreement
A pronoun matching the noun it replaces in number
Ambiguous pronoun
A pronoun that could refer to more than one noun
Its versus it's
The possessive versus the contraction of it is
Their, there, and they're
Possessive, location, and contraction of they are
Verb tense consistency
Keeping tense logical relative to the rest of the passage
Modifier placement
Putting a descriptive phrase next to what it describes
Dangling modifier
An opening phrase with no logical subject following it
Parallel structure
Items in a list sharing the same grammatical form
Apostrophe for possession
Adding apostrophe s for singular and s apostrophe for plural
